data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological evolution has no conscious goal of truth, whereas science explicitly aims at truth-likeness.","In sports, the rules remain constant; in science, the 'tests' (nature's challenges) can change fundamentally.","A biological survivor reproduces; a scientific theory only persists until falsified."],"overturn_conditions":["If nature is shown to be maliciously deceptive (e.g., changing laws specifically to fool our best theories), the pragmatic bet fails.","If it is proven that less-tested theories consistently solve new problems better than well-tested ones, the content-based preference is irrational."],"shared_structure":["Survival of the fittest does not guarantee future victory, only past resilience.","Choosing the current champion is rational because they have defeated the strongest opponents, not because they are invincible.","The goal is to find the strongest competitor, not to predict the outcome of the next match with certainty."],"source_memory_refs":["biological_natural_selection","championship_sports_tournaments"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we bet on the heavyweight champion despite knowing they can lose, we act on the best-corroborated theory despite knowing it might be false.","The rationality of the choice lies in the quality of the opposition defeated, not in the certainty of the result."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference that the future will resemble the past, but as a critical-rational decision rule to maximize the content of our conjectures while minimizing the risk of immediate error; however, accepting this defense costs us any guarantee of practical success, reducing scientific action to a gamble on the 'most informative survivor' without assurance that it will continue to survive.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the Tich\u00fd-Miller theorem holds that verisimilitude cannot be formally defined within Popper's framework, then the claim that we are approximating truth collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice between two unfalsified theories relies on the assumption that the one that survived severe tests is *more likely* to solve a new problem, then induction has been smuggled back in under the guise of 'content'.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's own admission that we must 'act' implies a belief in the stability of natural laws, then the distinction between corroboration and probability is merely semantic.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'Critical Pragmatism': since all theories are equally unproven (probability zero), the rational agent chooses the theory with the highest empirical content (best tested so far) because it offers the most opportunities for falsification and thus the fastest route to truth approximation (verisimilitude), whereas choosing a less-tested theory would be an arbitrary retreat from critical scrutiny. This avoids induction by treating corroboration as a historical report of survival, not a predictor of future performance.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
